summary: Defines a MIB for managing multiple logical and physical entities, such as chassis, cards, and modules, within a single SNMP agent. It was replaced by RFC 2737.

plainLanguage.summary: A big machine is made of many parts. This gives managers a parts list to look at the machine's pieces.

questions: how to list physical components via snmp
how do logical entities map to hardware
subtitle: Inventory of physical and logical components managed by one SNMP agent.

tldr.problem: Complex devices like stackable switches, modular routers, and multi-function systems contain many physical components (chassis, cards, ports, fans) and may manage multiple logical entities (separate routers or bridges). A single SNMP agent needs a way to describe both the physical structure and the logical entities it manages.
tldr.mechanism: Defines tables to list physical entities (with containment relationships, like which card is in which slot), logical entities (routers, bridges), and mappings between them, so a manager can understand the device structure and which logical entity controls which hardware.
tldr.outcome: Allows managers to discover and track hardware inventory, identify failing modules, and associate management functions (like a bridge instance) with their underlying hardware. Replaced by RFC 2737.

facts.label: Physical classes
facts.value: Chassis, Backplane, Container, Power Supply, Fan, Sensor, Module, Port (plus Other, Unknown)

facts.label: Logical entities supported
facts.value: Router, Bridge, Repeater, Terminal Server, and others

today: RFC 2037 is an Internet Standard but is obsoleted by RFC 2737, which provides a similar inventory model with extensions for alarm information and additional physical component types. The core concepts of physical containment hierarchies and logical-to-physical mappings remain in use.

sections.title: Multiple Entities in One Agent
sections.content:
Some network devices have become very complex. A modular router might have multiple line cards, each capable of running its own routing instance (separate OSPF areas). A stackable switch might have multiple physical switches stacked together, each logically independent. A terminal server might have separate logical entities for SNMP, console management, and packet forwarding.

Traditionally, each logical entity (like each router instance) needed its own SNMP agent. But this RFC recognizes that a single agent on a single device may manage many logical entities, and that each logical entity may depend on multiple physical components. The problem is: how does a manager discover what physical components exist, how they are organized, which logical entities depend on which hardware, and what to do when a module fails?
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a big machine with many cards inside. The manager wants to know: what cards are there, how are they arranged, and which program (router, bridge, etc.) uses each card?

sections.title: Physical and Logical Entities
sections.content:
The MIB defines two separate hierarchies: physical and logical entities.

Physical entities are hardware: the overall chassis (the root), backplanes, power supplies, fans, sensor modules, plug-in cards, and ports. Each is identified by an arbitrary index number and is described by a class (one of: chassis, backplane, power-supply, fan, sensor, module, port). A physical entity can be "contained in" another (for example, a card is contained in a slot, which is contained in the chassis).

Logical entities are management functions: routers, bridges, terminal servers, or repeaters. Each is identified by an index and has a name, type (e.g., router vs. bridge), and community string (for SNMP access). Multiple logical entities can exist within the same agent.

The containment tree for physical entities forms a hierarchy. For example: chassis (index 1) contains a backplane (index 2), which contains three slots (indices 3, 4, 5). Slot 3 contains a line card (index 6). Following the "contained in" pointers from the card up yields: card 6 is in slot 3, slot 3 is in backplane 2, backplane 2 is in chassis 1.
sections.plainLanguage: Physical entities are like a parts list: "The chassis contains a backplane, which has three slots, and slot 1 has a card in it." Logical entities are like job titles: "Router 1, Bridge 2, and Terminal Server 1 all run on this chassis."

sections.title: MIB Tables and Mappings
sections.content:
The Entity MIB consists of four main groups:

entityPhysical: The entPhysicalTable lists each physical component with its description, vendor type (an enterprise-specific identifier), general class, containment index, and relative position among siblings. For example, a power supply might be described as "Cisco 2821 PWR-2900-AC," classified as a power-supply, contained in the chassis, and in position 1 of the three power supplies.

entityLogical: The entLogicalTable lists each logical entity (router, bridge, etc.) with its name, description, type, and the community string (for SNMPv1) or other access parameters to use when querying that entity's view of the MIB.

entityMapping: Three mapping tables connect physical, logical, and other parts of the system. The entLPMappingTable maps logical entities to physical entities (which hardware does this router depend on?). The entAliasMappingTable associates logical and physical entities with identifiers from other MIBs (e.g., ifIndex for interfaces). The entPhysicalContainsTable provides a fast lookup of children for each parent physical entity.

entityGeneral: A scalar object entLastChangeTime records the sysUptime value when the physical or logical configuration last changed, helping managers detect when hardware was added or removed.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB has a parts table (physical), a roles table (logical), and tables that say "this part belongs to that job" and "this part has these interfaces."

sections.title: Examples: Routers and Repeaters
sections.content:
Stackable router example: A modular router with two line cards might have: a chassis (physical index 1), each line card as a module (indices 2 and 3), and ports on each card (indices 4, 5 for card 1; 6, 7 for card 2). Logically, there are two routers (indices 100 and 101), one per line card. entLPMappingTable shows that router 100 uses module 2, and router 101 uses module 3. entAliasMappingTable shows that port 4 is interface 1 in router 100's namespace, port 5 is interface 2 in router 100, and so on.

Repeater example: A building with many repeater segments connected via a central hub might be modeled as: a chassis (the hub), each repeater segment as a module, each port on each segment as a port entity. Logically, there is one repeater entity. Physical/logical mappings identify which ports belong to which segment and, via interface aliases, which repeater ports these are.
sections.plainLanguage: For a stacked system, the MIB shows: "Card A has ports 1-10, Card B has ports 11-20. Router A runs on Card A, Router B on Card B." For repeaters: "Segment 1 connects ports 1-8, Segment 2 connects ports 9-16, and so on."

sections.title: Agent Implementation and Constraints
sections.content:
An agent implementing this MIB must at minimum have one physical entity (the overall chassis or device). All MIB objects are read-only; no writing is allowed. This is a deliberate simplification to avoid the complexity of managing reconfiguration.

When multiple agents manage the same physical system, they are not required to be consistent or equivalent. Each agent may report a different view of the same physical components, depending on what the agent has access to. For example, a card-resident agent might report only components on that card, while a chassis-resident agent reports the entire system. Managers should not assume that different agents report identical indices or hierarchies.

The Entity MIB is designed as a single-scoped MIB: it returns the same object values regardless of which naming scope (community string, in SNMPv1 terms) the manager queries. This differs from multi-scoped MIBs like the Bridge or IP MIB, which may have different data per logical entity.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything is read-only. Each agent reports what it sees, which might be different from what another agent on the same system sees. The Entity MIB is always the same no matter which part of the system you ask.
